extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, historians, dramatists, and political scientists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing how democratic versus aristocratic conditions shape drama, historiography, parliamentary eloquence, and civic feelings; used to evaluate or produce political/literary works that respond to social condition. Emphasizes characteristics, causes, and effects of democracy on cultural and political forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama as the most democratic part of literature
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Theatre ... constitutes the most democratic part of their literature.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theatre requires neither preparation nor study and 'lays hold on you in the midst of your prejudices and your ignorance.' It brings together all classes (the higher ranks mix with the middle and the lower), and the audience (the pit) frequently imposes its taste on authors and even 'makes laws for the boxes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic subjects should concern the present age
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic peoples 'want to hear something which concerns themselves, and the delineation of the present age is what they demand.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When audiences are democratic they prefer plays about contemporary life rather than heroes and manners of antiquity; an author who persistently stages antiquity likely writes for a non-democratic (aristocratic) audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ancient subjects signals aristocratic dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘When the heroes and the manners of antiquity are frequently brought upon the stage ... that is enough to warrant a conclusion that the democratic classes have not yet got the upper hand of the theatres.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faithful observation of antiquated precedent in drama indicates the taste of an aristocratic class that still controls theatrical production and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocratic theatre selects high-born personages and stylized expression
rubrics_metrics.description: An aristocratic stage 'will only meet personages of quality, and share the emotions of kings' and is apt to 'impose upon dramatic authors certain modes of expression' that make the stage 'rise above nature and to go beyond it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristocratic drama tends to portray a limited set of virtues/vices and favors elevated style; it may therefore represent only one side of humanity or unrealistic characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic theatre depicts a medley of conditions and everyday truth
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘In democratic communities the spectators ... like to see upon the stage that medley of conditions, of feelings, and of opinions, which occurs before their eyes. The drama becomes more striking, more common, and more true.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democratic drama includes many social ranks and ordinary characters; it tends toward realism of contemporary life though may overemphasize minute singularities at the expense of general traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic drama licenses variety in subject choice and treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: When democratic classes rule the stage, 'they introduce as much license in the manner of treating subjects as in the choice of them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An expanding, diverse audience and many authors produce lack of concurrence on rules; dramatic conventions are questioned or abolished and each author/public may follow their whim, producing heterogeneous drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience in democracies prioritizes emotion and performance over literary correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Most playgoers 'do not go there to seek the pleasures of the mind, but the keen emotions of the heart. They do not expect to hear a fine literary work, but to see a play.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If characters excite curiosity and sympathy and the language is 'correctly enough to be understood,' audiences are satisfied; accuracy of style and strict probability of plot are less required since the chief merit is to affect the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability of plot is de-emphasized for novelty and rapidity
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘As for the probability of the plot, it is incompatible with perpetual novelty, surprise, and rapidity of invention. It is therefore neglected, and the public excuses the neglect.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic value in democratic theatres often derives from surprise, novelty and emotional effect rather than strict internal plausibility; audiences accept being brought to an affecting result 'by what road' the author chooses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popularity of the stage is shaped by social habits and censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: American stage popularity is limited by Puritan founding antipathy and municipal permission requirements for performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social origins, religious habits, and local laws (e.g., requiring municipal permission) shape how widely theatre is practiced and what authors produce; procedural constraints can indicate cultural attitudes toward drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historians in aristocratic ages attribute events to individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Historians who write in aristocratic ages 'refer all occurrences to the particular will or temper of certain individuals' and 'trace out the smallest causes with sagacity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristocratic historiography focuses on prominent actors, personal motives and discrete causes; the historian's task centers on detaching particular influences of great individuals from the broader mass of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historians in democratic ages emphasize general causes over individual agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Historians in democratic ages 'assign great general causes to all petty incidents' and attribute less influence to individuals over the destiny of the race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because individuals appear weaker in democratic societies, historians look for broad social, geographical, or civilizational causes, favoring explanations that operate on many people simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency in democratic historiography to construct systems and connect incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who write in democratic ages are 'given to connect incidents together, so as to deduce a system from them' and establish 'sequency and methodical order' among events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern historians often employ general theories to unify events into overarching systems; ancient historians, by contrast, produced fewer grand historical systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of determinism in democratic historical explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic historians sometimes 'deprive the people themselves of the power of modifying their own condition' and subject nations to 'an inflexible Providence' or 'some blind necessity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should avoid wholly denying individual or collective agency; useful analysis recognizes both general causes and particular influences—'one great portion' of events from general facts and another from special influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative behavior in democratic assemblies shaped by dependence on constituents
rubrics_metrics.description: In democratic countries a Representative 'becomes somebody from his position in the Assembly' and is 'perpetually haunted by a craving to acquire importance' before his constituents, causing him to obtrude his opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electoral insecurity drives representatives to speak frequently, address local grievances, and tailor language to constituents; laws increasing dependence on electors affect both conduct and speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituent expectations drive representatives to frequent, encompassing speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: Electors regard their Representative as 'the natural patron of the constituency' and expect him to be 'an orator' who compresses 'all the petty grievances' and the 'great questions of state' into speeches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representatives thus present a mix of grand general truths and petty minutiae in debates; the pressure to demonstrate capability at each occasion yields verbose orations aimed at electoral reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping silence can be the most useful parliamentary tactic (but is unpopular electorally)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘To keep silence is the most useful service that an indifferent spokesman can render to the commonwealth. Constituents, however, do not think so.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From a party/legislative effectiveness standpoint restraint is often optimal; democratic electoral pressures make silence politically costly even when strategically preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic assemblies tend toward vague and perplexed debates
rubrics_metrics.description: Because members attempt to address many local points and 'present to the mind of his auditors a succession of great general truths ... and of petty minutia,' 'the debates ... are frequently vague and perplexed' and 'seem rather to drag their slow length along than to advance towards a distinct object.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The institutional composition and electoral incentives of democracies encourage discursiveness and lack of focused deliberation; this is a recurrent evaluative feature of democratic legislatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: When addressing the nation, oratory attains breadth by appealing to general truths
rubrics_metrics.description: An orator in a democratic assembly 'speaks to the whole nation ... This expands his thoughts, and heightens his power of language' and he must 'have recourse to general truths derived from human nature' to resolve questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oratory that addresses universal human concerns can reach audiences beyond local boundaries; democratic debates have a potential grandeur when speakers frame matters in broadly human terms rather than narrow class privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic nations cherish equality more ardently than liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'first and most intense passion' engendered by equality is 'the love of that same equality,' and democratic nations are 'far more ardently and tenaciously attached to equality than to freedom.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons include: equality provides everyday, immediate pleasures accessible to all; equality seems more durable (harder to destroy) than political liberty; dangers of extreme equality are less apparent to most people, while dangers of liberty are immediate and more visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between equality and liberty and their historical relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality and freedom are distinct: 'equality may be established in civil society, without prevailing in the political world' and historically in many modern nations 'equality preceded freedom.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should distinguish social equality from political liberty; in some contexts equality's customs and habits predate political freedom, affecting how populations value each.
